claims.statement: Second-language speech fluency is multidimensional: speed, productivity, breakdown and repair features show different relationships with proficiency, so a single raw-speed metric is not a valid representation of the whole construct.

Perceived fluency is strongly associated with speed and pause frequency, less strongly with pause duration, and only weakly with repair measures; methodological choices moderate these relationships, so perceived fluency is not interchangeable with the full fluency construct.

Learners' first-language or personal speaking style contributes to observed second-language temporal fluency, especially breakdown behavior, so raw timing should not be interpreted as pure L2 mastery.
Underlying cognitive/processing fluency and observable utterance fluency are related but distinct, and their relationship varies with linguistic resource, processing speed and task demands.

Systematic practice can gradually automatize learned linguistic knowledge, but automatization is substantially skill-specific; performance gains in one operation or modality should not be assumed to transfer automatically to another.

Repeated task or topic performance can improve observable oral fluency and may support proceduralization, but faster performance on practiced material does not by itself establish flexible transfer to unfamiliar tasks or contexts.

Blocked, interleaved, massed and spaced practice schedules can produce different fluency outcomes and transfer patterns; current evidence does not support one schedule as uniformly best across all dimensions and learners.

Massed repetition can improve some breakdown-fluency measures while worsening speed or repair behavior on a novel task, demonstrating that optimizing one temporal metric can conceal meaningful trade-offs.
Distributed fluency practice can support later performance, but available evidence does not justify one universal spacing interval for fluency or automaticity training.

Instruction can strengthen collocational and multiword-sequence knowledge, and multiword-sequence use is associated with several oral-fluency dimensions; however, verbatim reuse of task-specific chunks is weaker evidence than flexible reuse across changed contexts.

Prompt, contextualized access to phonological vocabulary is associated with stronger L2 listening proficiency, but a training condition that improves target-word automaticity does not automatically establish superior gains in global listening proficiency.
Reading fluency should preserve comprehension and be demonstrated on unseen or changed text; faster performance on a repeatedly practiced passage is not equivalent to independent reading fluency.

Dialogue fluency includes the timing and coordination of turns, and turn gaps or overlap can influence perceived fluency; shortest-possible response latency is therefore not a universally valid interaction goal.

Pauses, repetitions, reformulations and repair should not be treated as uniformly negative: some reflect processing difficulty while others support monitoring, clarification and continued interaction.

Strong evidence of portable fluency or automaticity requires quality-preserving efficiency together with changed-task or changed-context performance and delayed evidence; timing improvement on practiced material alone is insufficient.

The readiness threshold, repetition dose, switch to variation, spacing, time pressure, reliable temporal measures and transfer criteria for Vietnamese adults near A0 are not established by the literature and require direct product validation.
